summary:
In March 2010, Malayalam professor T. J. Joseph set an exam question adapted from a published text. Because its character was named “Muhammed,” the passage was interpreted by some as insulting the Islamic Prophet. Protests followed, Joseph was charged under the Indian Penal Code, and his college suspended him.

On 4 July 2010, eight attackers stopped Joseph’s vehicle near his home in Muvattupuzha, severed his right hand and stabbed his thigh. He underwent a lengthy operation. The article identifies the attackers as members or associates of the Popular Front of India (PFI), an allegation the police investigated. Joseph said the question had been based on an approved text and that the character’s name referred to its author.

The college later reinstated Joseph’s suspension but dismissed him in September 2010, citing harm to religious sentiments. His wife, Salomi, died by suicide in March 2014; the article links her death to the family’s financial hardship and the prolonged failure to reinstate him.

Police arrested numerous suspects and filed charges against 27 PFI activists, including allegations of attempted murder and conspiracy. The National Investigation Agency said it did not plan to investigate, and the state government told the High Court investigators had found no evidence linking the PFI to several named international militant groups. One main accused, Savad, remained at large until his arrest in January 2024.

The attack was condemned by Kerala’s Assembly, Muslim organisations, Christian groups and others. Some Muslim organisations called it contrary to Islam and sought to isolate radical groups. Media commentary presented the assault as a grave attack on freedom of expression and warned of the dangers of religious extremism.
